newsitem.title: USA: Continental pilots target carrier's record profit.
newsitem.headline: Continental pilots target carrier's record profit.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc. posted record pre-tax profits and ended the first quarter with nearly $1 billion in cash on hand, fuelling renewed calls on Thursday for steep pay increases from the carrier's pilots.

Negotiators with the Houston-based airline held talks in Washington, D.C., this week drafting terms of a new contract with its pilots union, which is holding out for a wage increase of up to 38 percent and improved benefits.
"We are going to do something that is fair to our pilots and fair to every other employee, and that's all I want to say about it," Continental Chairman Gordon Bethune said.

Negotiators this week made "fair progress" on issues like seniority and other non-economic terms of the contract, but there have been no discussions to date on the pilots' demand for sharply higher wages, improved benefits and work concessions, union officials said.

"It's difficult to qualify just how far apart we are," said Captain Bill Borrelli, vice president of the Independent Association of Continental Pilots. He said talks were not in danger of breaking down, and both sides still expected to complete a contract by July 1.

"We are not heading down the same road as American at this point in time," he said, referring to talks between American Airlines and its pilots that prompted a strike call and intervention by President Clinton.
Continental, which navigated its way out of bankruptcy in 1993, posted its eighth straight record quarterly profits with $124 million of pre-tax income.

Net profits, however, fell to $74 million, or $1.13 a share, from $88 million, or $1.35 a share, in the year-ago period. Fully diluted earnings per share slid to 95 cents from $1.18, exceeding analysts' consensus estimate of 89 cents.
Continental stock was up 37.5 cents at $32.75 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

Earnings were trimmed in large part because the airline booked $46 million in tax provisions in the 1997 first quarter compared with $2 million in the same period last year, Chief Financial Officer Larry Kellner said.

The nation's fifth-largest carrier, Continental ended the first quarter with a cash balance of $927 million, up from $657 million in 1996 and well above its internal target of $750 million, executives said.

The airline during the quarter closed $707 million in financing tied to the acquisition of 30 new Boeing aircraft scheduled for delivery between March 1997 and February 1998 and a $160 million revolving facility to fund pre-delivery for new airplanes for delivery through 1999.
"Getting our borrowing costs in line is really what allowed us to grow and grow profitably," Kellner said.
First-quarter passenger revenues rose 14 percent to $1.6 billion on 9 percent higher capacity, while operating income increased 22 percent to $146 million, the carrier said.

Revenue per available seat mile, an industry benchmark of cost efficiency, edged up 0.45 cent to 10.22 cents. Continental's March load factor of 74.5 percent and its yield in February were the highest ever in the Houston-based company's 63-year history, it said.
"We continue to switch from backpacks and flip flops to coats and ties," President Greg Brenneman said of the more profitable business travelers flying Continental.
